description: A village irrigation crew initially coordinates gate openings by passing instructions from person to person. Because each resident can privately recall a particular exchange through at most three subsequent interpersonal exchanges, long conversational chains are unreliable: ordinary conversations can erase an instruction before the required action occurs. The crew therefore reorganizes coordination around the communal inscription room. Instead of recording a detailed sequence of future commands that may become stale, residents use their daily ten-minute visit to inscribe a small set of pending irrigation states: which gate action has most recently been durably confirmed, which action should occur next, and whether a known condition requires the sequence to pause. A resident who reads that the eastern gate is next can perform the action and, if their daily room visit remains available afterward, later inscribe the new confirmed state. Short verbal exchanges still bridge gaps between visits, but any instruction dependent on private recall must be acted upon before more than three subsequent interpersonal exchanges occur. This produces an unexpected coordination rhythm. Progress through a multi-person task is no longer primarily limited by how quickly villagers can talk; it is limited by opportunities to convert transient coordination into persistent shared state. Residents begin conserving their single room visit strategically. Visiting early provides current information but sacrifices the ability to record developments discovered later. Delaying the visit preserves an opportunity to publish a later state change but leaves the resident dependent on short-lived verbal information beforehand. Different roles therefore develop different useful visit timings even without any formal scheduler: residents expected to initiate morning actions benefit from early visits, while those expected to confirm later actions benefit from retaining access until later in the day. The system also favors coordination protocols in which each durable inscription describes the presently confirmed state and a limited next action rather than requiring residents to reconstruct a long conversational history. This does not eliminate gaps. If someone acts after using their daily visit, the completed action may remain absent from the communal inscription until an informed resident with unused access records it, and verbal knowledge of the action can disappear if it is not transferred or acted upon within the recall ceiling. Thus repeated coordination produces a scarce resource that did not exist explicitly in the original arrangement: not merely inscription-room time, but the option value of an unused daily visit. Villagers must coordinate both the irrigation work and when they consume their only opportunity to read and alter durable shared state.
